title.en: The Kumulipo: The Genealogical Chant of Cosmic Birth
title.zh: 《庫姆利波》：宇宙誕生之系譜頌歌

region.en: Hawaii Island (Ka'u district of the chant's origin; symbolic pin at Hilo)
region.zh: 夏威夷島（頌歌源於卡烏地區；象徵性定位於希洛）

texts.period: Composed c. 1700 CE for Kalanikauikeaouli? (chant for the birth of the high chief Ka-I-i-mamao); recorded by Queen Liliuokalani, translation 1897; manuscript tradition 19th c. (Bishop Museum)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Liliuokalani translation, 1897) / Bishop Museum (oral ms)
source.work: Kumulipo, trans. Queen Liliuokalani, An Hawaiian Legend of the Creation, San Francisco 1897 (public domain); Martha Beckwith, Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant, Honolulu 1951

summary.en: At the time of deep darkness, life is born from the Kumulipo (the deep source) in sixteen waves of genealogical pairs — coral, fish, birds, insects, plants, then humans — each sea-organism paired with its land counterpart, until WAKEA the ancestor appears and the human lineage descends to the chanting chief: creation as whakapapa-like genealogy, not narrative.
summary.zh: 於深暗之時，生命自庫姆利波（深源）生，凡十六波系譜之對——珊瑚、魚、鳥、蟲、植物、而後人類——海中生物與陸上生物一一成對，直至祖先瓦凱亞出現，人系下延至誦唱之酋長：創世為系譜而非敘事。

sensitivity.note: The Kumulipo is a sacred chiefly genealogy; living Hawaiian communities (ali'i descendants, sovereignty discourse) treat it with care; prefer community-authored scholarship.

passages.text: Liliuokalani translation (1897), opening lines (public domain): 'When the light of day was dim, and the night of Kumulipo was being born; when the light of day was dim, and the night of Pō'ele was being born... of the Pola'i, of the Ha'ele? of the deep darknesses, the Po was born.'

Condensed paraphrase of the first wā (Beckwith 1951 base): Born of the night, the coral polyp; born of the night, the small fry that swim in the sea's shallows; born of the night, the echinoderm? and on land its pair — each sea creature paired with a land creature through seven wā, until the fourth? until men are born of the night and Wakea's line begins. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the first wā (Beckwith 1951 base); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Queen Liliuokalani, An Hawaiian Legend of the Creation, 1897 (public domain); Martha Beckwith, Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant, Honolulu 1951 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Kumulipo is the royal cosmogonic chant of Hawaii — over 2,000 lines of genealogical verse chanted at the birth of the high chief Ka-I-i-mamao (c. 1700) to graft his lineage onto the origin of all things. It is a cosmogony as genealogy: the world is not made but born, in sixteen wā (waves/generations), each verse pairing a sea-being with its land twin.

THE SIXTEEN WAVES. The chant opens in the time of Po, the deep darkness: 'When the light of day was dim, and the night of Kumulipo was being born...' — creation begins in seven darknesses (Kumulipo, Pō'ele, Pō'eli...), the deep source out of which life emerges. The first wā brings the coral polyp and the small fry of the shallows; the second the fish of the deep; each sea-being born 'of the night' is paired with its land counterpart — the sea pig with the land pig, the sea banana with the land banana, the sea taro with the land taro — the paired taxonomy by which Hawaiian thought classifies the world. Through the wā life rises: fish, birds, insects, reptiles? plants; then in the middle wā the age of humans begins — humans born of the night in successive generations — and in the final waves the great ancestral figures appear: Wakea ('sky-father') and Papa ('earth-mother'), the divine siblings whose union founds the human line, and the chiefly line descends — through Kāne? through the generations of chiefs — until the chant arrives at Ka-I-i-mamao himself: the newborn chief is the latest born of all things, his mana continuous with the coral polyp.

FUNCTIONS. The Kumulipo grounds Hawaiian chiefly legitimacy (the newborn chief's genealogy is the cosmos), the ecology of pairing (land-sea reciprocity — the fishpond and the garden as ritual twins), the kapu system's logic (Wakea and Papa's family laws — the 'Ulu? the breadfruit child episode — ground gender and eating taboos), and the modern sovereignty discourse (Liliuokalani's 1897 translation, made while deposed, is itself a political act: the nation's genealogy against annexation). It is chanted in hula hālau, taught in Hawaiian immersion schools, and cited in land claims; its sixteen waves are recited at the Makahiki new year and at royal commemorations, keeping the genealogy itself a living liturgy.

PROVENANCE. The chant was recorded in the 19th century (Bishop Museum manuscript tradition; the Liliuokalani translation made in exile); Beckwith's 1951 edition is the scholarly base. Prefer contemporary Hawaiian scholarship (e.g. Puakea Nogelmeier's Awaiaulu projects; Ku'ulei Higashi Kanaehe? — community-authored work) in citation.
narrative.zh: 《庫姆利波》為夏威夷王族宇宙頌歌，凡二千餘行，於約1700年高酋 Ka-I-i-mamao 誕生時誦唱，將其世系接於萬物之源。創世為系譜：世界非造而是生，凡十六波（wā），每節海中生物與陸上生物成對。頌歌啟於波之深暗：『當晝光漸暗，庫姆利波之夜誕生時……』——生命自七重黑暗之深源生出。第一波生珊瑚蟲與淺灘小魚；第二波生深海之魚；凡夜中所生之海中物皆與陸上物成對——海中之豬配陸上之豬、海中蕉配陸上蕉、海芋配陸芋——此即夏威夷思想分類世界之對偶法。歷波而上：魚、鳥、蟲、植物；至中波而人類之紀始；末波出現大祖瓦凱亞（天父）與帕帕（地母），其兄妹之結合開人系；酋長世系下延至新生酋長本人——酋長為萬物中最晚生者，其瑪那與珊瑚蟲相續。功能：酋長合法性之根基、海陸互惠之生態觀、卡普制度之邏輯（瓦凱亞與帕帕之家法釋性別與飲食禁忌）、以及現代主權論述（利留卡拉尼女王於被廢之年譯之，為抵抗兼併之政治行為）。

functions: Charter of chiefly legitimacy: the newborn chief's genealogy is the cosmos
Ecology of pairing: land-sea reciprocity as ritual taxonomy
Kapu logic: Wakea and Papa's family laws ground gender and eating taboos
Sovereignty discourse: Liliuokalani's 1897 translation as political act

variants.name: Liliuokalani translation (1897)
variants.summary: The Queen's own English rendering, framed as Hawaiian national document against annexation — historically the most politicized version.

variants.name: Beckwith edition (1951)
variants.text_tradition: Martha Beckwith, Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant, Honolulu
variants.summary: The scholarly critical edition with Hawaiian text, wā divisions, and comparative Polynesian apparatus — the academic base text.

variants.name: Bishop Museum manuscript tradition
variants.summary: The recorded chant-manuscripts (19th c. chiefly schools and missions) preserve variant lines; textual scholarship continues on their collation.

variants.name: Polynesian parallels (Kumulipo vs. Maori whakapapa)
variants.text_tradition: Maori genealogical chants; Tuamotuan creation songs
variants.summary: The genealogical-cosmogony form is pan-Polynesian (Maori whakapapa to Rangi and Papa; Tuamotuan Kiho-tumu) — the Kumulipo is its Hawaiian royal elaboration.

primary_sources.citation: Chant composed c. 1700 CE for the birth of Ka-I-i-mamao; recorded 19th c. (Bishop Museum MSS). Translations: Queen Liliuokalani, An Hawaiian Legend of the Creation, San Francisco 1897 (public domain); Martha Beckwith, Kumulipo, Honolulu 1951 (copyright).

secondary_sources.citation: Beckwith 1940, New Haven: Yale University Press — the Kumulipo in Hawaiian mythic corpus context.
Nogelmeier 2010s, Honolulu: Awaiaulu — contemporary Hawaiian-language scholarship on 19th-c. Hawaiian texts (community-authored).

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Kumulipo is a sacred chiefly genealogy; use Liliuokalani 1897 (public domain) and community-authored Hawaiian scholarship; do not excerpt chiefly sections casually; be aware of sovereignty discourse when citing the translation's political frame.

title.en: Ti'iti'i and the Earthquake God: The Samoan Theft of Fire
title.zh: 蒂伊蒂伊與地震之神：薩摩亞盜火記

region.zh: 薩摩亞薩瓦伊島（地震之神馬富耶之域）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded 19th c. (George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago, London 1884; John B. Stair, Old Samoa, 1897)

source.work: George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, London 1884 (public domain); John B. Stair, Old Samoa, London 1897 (public domain)

summary.en: Ti'iti'i, son of the woman Talanga, descends to the underworld to demand fire from the earthquake-god Mafuie; beaten, he returns, catches Mafuie's tail in a crack, and fights him; he breaks off one of Mafuie's arms, the source of earthquakes, and carries the firesticks to mankind — the Samoan variant of the Maui fire-theft cycle.
summary.zh: 蒂伊蒂伊（塔蘭加之子）下冥府向地震神馬富耶索火；被擊而返，夾其尾於石縫而鬥；折斷馬富耶致地震之一臂，攜取火之木歸於人類——此為毛伊盜火圈之薩摩亞變體。

sensitivity.note: Living Samoan tradition (fa'asamoa); recordings are 19th-c. missionary-era collections — flagged.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884): Talanga told her son Ti'iti'i that Mafuie kept fire in the underworld; Ti'iti'i went down, demanded fire, was beaten, came back with a broken arm — and his mother said: 'go again, and catch him by the tail when the earthquake shakes the ground.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884) (ending): Ti'iti'i caught Mafuie by the tail and held him in a crack of rock; they fought, and Ti'iti'i broke off one of Mafuie's arms — 'wherefore earthquakes are less violent than of old' — and Mafuie surrendered the firesticks; Ti'iti'i carried them up, and fire belonged to mankind. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Turner (1884) (ending); not verbatim.

texts.language: Samoan (Gagana Samoa; recorded in English translation)
texts.canonical_translation: George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Samoan fire-theft is the western Polynesian variant of the Māui cycle (cross-ref maori-maui) — with a distinct hero and a distinct cosmology of earthquake.

BEGINNING: THE MOTHER'S INSTRUCTION. In Savai'i, fire is the secret of the earthquake-god Mafuie, who keeps it in the underworld (his domain is the volcano region of Savai'i, the Saleaula? the volcanic district). Talanga, the mortal woman married to the gods, tells her son Ti'iti'i ('the smashed? the striker') that men eat their food raw because Mafuie hoards fire: 'go down and get fire for us.'

MIDDLE: THE FIGHT WITH MAFUIE. Ti'iti'i descends to the underworld and demands fire; Mafuie refuses — fire is the gods' — and beats the youth. Ti'iti'i returns broken-armed to his mother, who gives him the strategy of the trickster: 'Mafuie's tail is his strength; when the earthquake shakes, catch him by the tail.' Ti'iti'i goes down again, and when the ground quakes he seizes Mafuie by the tail and holds him fast in a crack of rock; the two wrestle until Ti'iti'i breaks off one of Mafuie's arms — the arm with which Mafuie shook the earth — 'and hence earthquakes are less violent than they were of old' (the aition of Samoa's lessened quakes, tied to Savai'i's volcanism).

END: FIRE FOR MANKIND. Defeated, Mafuie surrenders the firesticks (the ritual fire-plough of Polynesian fire-making); Ti'iti'i carries them up to the world of men, and from that day mankind cooks its food and kindles fire — the western-Polynesian answer to the Maui-Mahuika tale (in the Māori telling the hero is Maui, the fire-keeper the goddess Mahuika; in Samoa the fire-keeper is male and the loss is an arm). The narrative's twins (Talanga's family) and the volcano geography root it in Samoan chiefly genealogy and the geology of Savai'i.

COMPARATIVE AND FUNCTIONAL NOTE. Set beside the Maori telling (Maui against the fire-goddess Mahuika, whose fingernails are flames) and the Hawaiian telling (Maui snaring the sun on Haleakala; the alae hen guarding fire), the Samoan variant shows the cycle's grammar: a young hero of double descent, a fire-keeper of the chthonic world, a trick to break the monopoly, and an aition written into the landscape. In Samoa the aition is geological — the broken arm of Mafuie explains why quakes gentled — and the firesticks ground the ritual fire-plough (the si? the 'tili aila) that Turner describes as still practiced. The narrative is told in chiefly oratory (fa'alupega) contexts where Savai'i's descent lines claim the tale; Turner's missionary collection preserved it in English at the cost of its liturgical setting — a caution this record flags.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative aitiologizes fire-by-friction (the firesticks), the diminished violence of Samoan earthquakes, and the geography of Savai'i's volcanic district; it structures the Samoan trickster-hero cycle and the chiefly genealogies that claim descent from Talanga's line; and it is the standard Samoan comparandum in Polynesian myth studies (Turner's 1884 collection being the missionary-era base text — flagged).
narrative.zh: 薩摩亞盜火記為毛伊圈之西玻里尼西亞變體。薩瓦伊島上，火為地震神馬富耶之秘藏於冥府；凡女塔蘭加告其子蒂伊蒂伊：世人食生食，因馬富耶吝火——『去為我們取火來。』蒂伊蒂伊下冥府索火，馬富耶拒而擊之；蒂伊蒂伊斷臂而歸，母授詭計：『地震搖動時，抓其尾。』再下，乘地震之際夾其尾於石縫，相搏至折斷馬富耶致震之一臂——『故地震較古時為輕』（薩瓦伊火山地震減弱之釋義）。馬富耶降，交出取火之木；蒂伊蒂伊攜火上界，人類自茲熟食取火——與毛利本中英雄為毛伊、守火者為女神瑪胡伊卡相對，薩摩亞版守火者為男、所失者為臂。功能：鑽木取火之釋義、地震減弱之釋義、薩瓦伊火山地理之敘事化、以及酋長世系（塔蘭加之後）之憲章。

functions: Aition of fire-by-friction: the firesticks passed to mankind
Aition of diminished Samoan earthquakes: Mafuie's broken arm
Geography of Savai'i's volcanic district mythologized
Polynesian comparative hero-cycle (Samoan variant of the Maui fire-theft)

title.en: Qat of the Banks Islands: The Culture Hero of Vanuatu
title.zh: 班克斯群島之卡特：瓦努阿圖文化英雄

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore, Oxford 1891 (public domain)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore, Oxford 1891 (public domain), chs. on Qat and Mota narratives

summary.en: Qat, born of a stone and raised by his mother's brothers, creates the islands, men, and pigs, kills the night with a joke, teaches the Suqe graded society, and departs in a canoe said to return — the great culture hero of the northern Vanuatu archipelago.
summary.zh: 卡特效生於石、由母舅養大；造島嶼、人類與豬，以戲言終結長夜，創立蘇蓋等級會社，後乘獨木舟而去，傳言將返——此為瓦努阿圖北部群島之大文化英雄。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the 1891 Codrington collection (missionary-era; flagged); living Vanuatu communities (kastom movement) hold the heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891), Qat narratives: Qat was born of a stone, which split? he emerged as a boy; his mother's brothers raised him; he made pigs, made men? he carved wooden figures and beat drums until the wood opened and living men stepped out — 'thus men came.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891), Qat narratives; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891) (the night): In the beginning night was long, longer than the day; Qat bought? he took a cock from the Night-man (Qong? Qat's brother), waited for the dawn-cock's crow, and killed the Night-man — 'so the night became short, as it now is.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Codrington (1891) (the night); not verbatim.

texts.language: Mota (Banks Islands language), recorded in English
texts.canonical_translation: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, Oxford 1891 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Qat (Qat) is the culture hero of the Banks Islands (northern Vanuatu), recorded by the missionary-anthropologist R. H. Codrington in the 1880s-90s — the fullest Melanesian hero corpus in print.

BEGINNING: THE STONE-BORN BOY. Qat was born of a stone (in some tellings of the great rock of Gaua); his mother's brothers raised him. From boyhood he shows the maker's power: he makes pigs from? he goes about creating — islands of the archipelago, the reef, the forest.

MIDDLE: THE MAKING OF MEN AND PIGS. The great creative acts: Qat carves figures of wood (or dris? of dracaena wood), beats drums beside them until the wood splits and living men and women step out — 'thus men came into the world'; he makes pigs, coconuts, and gardens; he teaches the Suqe, the graded men's society (the pig-killing grade system that organizes Banks-Islands status) — culture is Qat's curriculum. His brothers (or shadow-rivals, the Qat-qaravu? the eleven brothers including Qat the trickster) parody his works — making bad men? bad pigs — and Qat must undo or outdo them (the Melanesian theme of defective creativity).

END: THE KILLING OF THE NIGHT AND THE DEPARTURE. Night (Qong? the long night) originally lasted longer than day; Qat goes to the Night-man (his brother in some tellings), buys a cock? waits hidden until the dawn-cock crows, and slays the Night-man — 'and so night became short, as now it is' — the aition of day and night's balance. Qat then departs: he sails away in a canoe for the horizon, and the Mota tradition says he went to? that he will return — the departed hero whose return is hoped (Codrington records the missionary-era debate: Qat identified with the returning Christ by some converts, and with the departed ancestral power by others). In the Torres Islands? the adjacent traditions, Qat's mother? the variants across the Banks group differ on his relations and his wives (the Ro Leiq? the Ambae? — the neighboring island traditions have their own heroes, Tagaro of the New Hebrides? cross-ref tagaro-sea).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds the Suqe graded society (pig-killing ranks as Qat's institution), the aition of day/night, the creative ethics of Melanesian culture heroes (making by carving and drum-beat; parody and defective twins), and the kastom movement's hero canon in modern Vanuatu; Codrington's collection remains the printed base (missionary-era, flagged), with contemporary Vanuatu Cultural Centre fieldwork (kastom narratives recorded in Bislama and Mota) as the living source.
narrative.zh: 卡特（Qat）為瓦努阿圖北部班克斯群島之文化英雄，柯德林頓（1880-90年代）採錄之敘事為印刷文獻中之美拉尼西亞英雄敘事最富者。卡特自大石而生（一說生於高阿島巨巖），由母舅養大；自幼即顯造物之力：造群島、礁、林。其大功：刻木為像，擊鼓於側，木裂而活人步出——『人由此而來』；造豬、椰、園圃；創立蘇蓋男子等級會社（殺豬進階之制度）——文化即卡特之課程。其諸兄（或影響之對手）仿其作而皆劣（美拉尼西亞『殘缺創造』之題）。太初夜長於晝；卡特至夜之主人（一說其兄）處，候晨雞初啼而殺之——『故夜短如今日』（晝夜之釋義）。後卡特乘獨木舟駛向海平線而去，莫塔島傳統言其將返——柯德林頓記錄了宣教時代之爭：歸化者或以卡特擬復臨之基督，或以其為先祖之力。功能：蘇蓋等級會社之創立、晝夜釋義、美拉尼西亞文化英雄之創造倫理（刻木擊鼓而造人）、以及現代瓦努阿圖『卡斯通』運動之英雄正典。

functions: Institutional charter: the Suqe graded society as Qat's teaching
Aition of day and night: the killing of the long Night
Melanesian creative ethics: making by carving and drum-beat; parody-twins
Kastom movement hero canon in modern Vanuatu

variants.name: Codrington's Mota collection (1891)
variants.text_tradition: The Melanesians, chs. on Qat (missionary-anthropologist, Melanesian Mission)
variants.summary: The printed base text: stone-birth, wooden figures, drum creation, the killing of the long night, the departure by canoe.

variants.name: Tagaro of the New Hebrides/Vanuatu (cross-island variants)
variants.text_tradition: Neighboring island traditions (Ambae, Maewo; see base record tagaro-sea)
variants.summary: Tagaro (Tagar) is the cognate culture hero of Ambae and Maewo — a rival/parallel maker whose narratives displace Qat's southward; the two canons meet in the archipelago.

variants.name: Suqe society ritual tradition
variants.summary: The pig-killing grade ladder practiced into the 20th-21st c. preserves Qat's institutional memory as living rite rather than story.
